At this year's World Cup finals, more than 23% of players—almost one in four—were not born in the country they represent, setting a new record in both proportion and numbers. Among the 48 participating teams, eight have a majority of players born overseas. Curaçao, a constituent country of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, has a population even smaller than that of Wan Chai, yet only one player on the entire squad was born locally: their most marketable player, Tahith Chong, who has Cantonese heritage and was developed at Sheffield United; all the other players come from the Netherlands itself.

The stark disparities at the World Cup not only deliver tension and excitement for fans but also put national football associations in a dilemma—they need star players to draw attention, yet they also want broadcasters from smaller nations to get exposure, and pleasing both sides at once is no easy task. This tournament has been plagued by controversy: fans have mockingly dubbed the heavily promoted stars "FIFA kids," and representatives of several teams have lodged post-match complaints with their respective federations about the standard of officiating. For fans, when they look back on the classic matches of the 2026 World Cup years from now, what may be most memorable is not the final itself, but a thrilling last-16 encounter in which defending champions Argentina edged Cape Verde 3-2. Cape Verde's 40-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha repeatedly produced stunning saves against shots from Messi, becoming the focus of global attention overnight and now boasting nearly 30 million fans worldwide. For players from small nations, being able to compete on equal terms with legendary stars on the world's biggest sporting stage through their own ability is the glory that truly belongs to them.

On the eve of the previous World Cup, FIFA wrote to all participating teams, earnestly asking each side to "let football be the protagonist" and urging that the tournament not be drawn into any ideological or political struggles. That World Cup was still hosted by a single country, with 32 national teams taking part. The next edition will mark the centenary of the tournament and will, for the first time ever, span three continents, co-hosted by six countries.
